newsitem.title: QATAR: Total eyes stake in Qatar refinery.
newsitem.headline: Total eyes stake in Qatar refinery.

text.p: Total SA Chairman Thierry Desmarest said on Tuesday his company was trying to take a stake in a condensate refinery in the tiny Gulf Arab state of Qatar.

"We are trying to take a share in a condensate refinery in Qatar," he told reporters, but did not specify how large a stake the company was bidding for, or how high the capacity of the proposed refinery would be.
"It's all a bit too early to say anything because negotiations are going on," he said.
Qatar has planned to set up a condensate refinery at Ras Laffan, the site of a string of multi-billion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) and other hydrocarbon-based projects.

The U.S. Mobil Corp, which dominates the state's gas sector with a 10 percent stake in Qatar Liquefied Gas Company (Qatargas) and 26.5 percent in Ras Laffan LNG Company (Rasgas), has also shown interest in the refinery project.
Qatar currently produces around 80,000 barrels a day of condensates -- mainly exported to the Far East. But the figure is expected to soar to more than 200,000 bpd by 2000.
"We are proposing to design the refinery adequate enough to utilise all the condensates produced from the North Field," Desmarest said.

Condensates are hydrocarbon gases that are heavier than liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) but lighter than crude oil and are rich in naphtha, diesel and jet fuel but the extraction of these lucrativ petroleum products is expensive.

The North Field, known to contain more than 500 trillion cubic feet of gas-in-place and 380 trillion cubic feet of recoverable reserves, is the world's largest single concentration of natural gas. It gives Qatar the third largest gas reserves in the world after Russia and Iran.
Desmarest said Total, which has a 20 percent stake in Qatargas's upstream activities and 10 percent in downstream, was keen to expand its operations in Qatar's oil and gas sector.
But he said the company was unable to sell Qatari gas in Europe because of "big price differences at present".

"The price of gas in Japan, South Korea and other Far East countries is 40 percent higher than in Europe, mainly because of the transportation cost involved. The Far East has to import gas from a long distance and Europe has indigenous supply from the North Sea," he said.
